meta.theme: the impossibility of believing at will traced to what believing is rather than to any weakness of the will, and then confined, since attention and company are voluntary and do alter belief over time, while the indirect route only places a person where a belief may arrive, so that the looking can be demanded and the landing cannot

meta.reviewer_notes: A short conceptual argument followed by three qualifications, the third of which cuts against the first two. Readers who take the opening claim as the passage's position over-answer the characterisation question; readers who take the qualifications as a retreat under-answer it. The division between what can be asked and what cannot is stated only in the final three sentences.
meta.tone: spare, argumentative, scrupulous in its limits

quality.adversarial_review: Q1's live rival is the option that beliefs arrive by accident and have nothing to do with what a person does, which the fourth paragraph forbids by saying attention and company alter belief slowly and unreliably; the phrase marks the absence of a guarantee, not the absence of a connection. Q2's rival is the option that what a person believes can be altered by what he attends to, which is the passage's own qualification and therefore a claim it argues for rather than a premise it needs; negating it leaves the conceptual argument of the second paragraph untouched. Q3's rival is the option calling the passage an argument that religious demands are incoherent, which is the use the third paragraph describes and then refuses. Q4's rival is the option that a person who attends properly and still does not believe has failed in something, which the fifth paragraph denies in the sentence saying nothing in his attending guarantees an outcome.

passage.title: The Thing You Cannot Hand Over

paragraphs.text: Try, at this moment, to believe that there is a second moon. Not to imagine one, not to say there is one, not to behave as though there were: to believe it, which is to take it that there is. You will find that you cannot, and the interesting question is what sort of failure that is. It is not a failure that more effort would repair, and it is not a weakness peculiar to you. It belongs with trying to become taller by deciding to be.

The explanation lies in what believing is. To believe something is to take it that it is so, and that is why the only considerations able to move a belief are considerations bearing on whether it is so. Evidence can move it. An argument can move it. The testimony of somebody who was there can move it. What cannot move it is the attractiveness of the conclusion, because attractiveness is not a report about the world and the mind has no way of using it as one. Offer a man a large sum to believe in the second moon and you have given him a powerful motive and no reason whatever, and the motive has nothing to work on. The inability is not psychological. It follows from the job the state is doing.

This is usually produced in order to dispose of something larger. If belief cannot be chosen, the argument runs, then a demand to believe is a demand nobody is able to meet, and a tradition that makes such demands is asking the impossible of its members. The premise is sound. The conclusion does not follow from it, and three things need saying.

The first is that the claim covers the moment of assent and nothing else. Almost everything a religion actually asks of a person is voluntary: where he goes on a given morning, what he reads and declines to read, whose company he keeps, what he gives an hour a day to. All of these alter, slowly and unreliably, what a person ends up believing. Belief is unchosen; it is not unmanaged. The second is that this leaves a believer open to appraisal rather than beyond it. A man who has arranged never to meet an argument against his position has done something he can be asked about, and what he did was voluntary even if what he now thinks is not.

The third point is the one that keeps the qualification honest. The indirect route is not a slower way of choosing a belief. It is a way of putting oneself where a belief may happen to one, and the difference is not a nicety. A person who attends properly may end where he began, or somewhere he had no wish to go, and nothing in his attending guarantees the outcome. From which a division follows that ought to be kept. What can be asked of somebody is the looking. What cannot be asked is the landing. A tradition that says go and study, sit with these people, give this an hour a day for a year has asked for something a person can do, and fail at, and be judged on. A tradition that says believe this has asked for something nobody can hand over, however willing.

questions.target_mistake: reading a phrase that denies a guarantee as one that denies any connection between what a person does and what he comes to believe
questions.prediction_target: The learner should paraphrase from the sentences around it: the attending is up to him and the result is not.
questions.stem: In saying that the indirect route puts a person where a belief may happen to him, the author chiefly means that

options.A: beliefs arrive by accident and have nothing to do with anything a person actually does
options.B: the attending can be undertaken, and what it leads to cannot be settled beforehand
options.C: a person may end up believing something that he would much rather not believe
options.D: belief is produced by circumstance and is therefore not the believer's responsibility

explanation.expert_notice: The phrase is explained by the sentence that follows it. A person who attends properly may end where he began, or somewhere he had no wish to go, and nothing in his attending guarantees the outcome. The paragraph before has already said the voluntary acts do alter belief, slowly and unreliably.
explanation.correct_reasoning: The correct option separates what a person controls from what he does not, which is exactly what the phrase is placed there to do. The looking is his; where it deposits him is not, and that gap is the reason the final sentences can ask for one and refuse to ask for the other. The word may is doing all the work, and it denies certainty rather than denying influence.
explanation.question_type_note: A phrase-in-context question is settled by the sentences that surround the phrase. Where an author writes may, check whether he is removing a guarantee or removing a connection; they read alike and mean different things.
explanation.reading_habit: When a phrase seems to weaken an author's own argument, look at the paragraph before it. Writers set limits against a claim they have just made, and the limit is almost never as large as it looks in isolation.

distractors.why_wrong: The paragraph before states the connection plainly: what he reads, whose company he keeps and what he attends to all alter what he ends up believing. The phrase removes the guarantee and leaves the influence standing.
distractors.seductive_element: It is the live rival, because happen to one really does suggest an event befalling a passive person, and the passage has just denied that belief can be chosen.

distractors.why_wrong: The passage does say a person may end somewhere he had no wish to go, but that is one case among several and it is offered as an illustration of the missing guarantee rather than as the meaning of the phrase, which concerns what can and cannot be secured.
distractors.seductive_element: It restates a clause that sits three words away from the phrase, which makes it feel like the closest possible paraphrase.

distractors.why_wrong: The paragraph before insists on the opposite, saying the position leaves a believer open to appraisal rather than beyond it, and that a man who arranged never to meet an argument has done something he can be asked about.
distractors.seductive_element: Anything a person does not choose is usually taken to be something he cannot be blamed for, and the passage's own language of happening invites the excuse.

questions.target_mistake: naming one of the passage's later qualifications as a premise of the argument it qualifies
questions.prediction_target: The learner should be able to state the gap first: the argument needs it to be true that wanting something does not bear on whether it is so.
questions.stem: The argument of the second paragraph depends on which of the following assumptions?

options.A: That religious traditions have always demanded assent rather than any particular practice
options.B: That no human being has ever managed to believe something purely by deciding to
options.C: That what a person believes can be altered by what he chooses to give his attention to
options.D: That a thing's being desirable to believe is not itself a reason for thinking it true

explanation.expert_notice: The paragraph moves in three steps. Believing is taking it that something is so; therefore only what bears on whether it is so can move a belief; therefore attractiveness cannot. The last step is the one with a gap under it, and the gap is the status of attractiveness as a consideration.
explanation.correct_reasoning: The correct option fills that gap, and negating it destroys the argument. If desirability did bear on truth, then the offer of a large sum would supply a reason and not merely a motive, and the second moon could be believed in by anyone sufficiently well paid. The paragraph's own words mark the assumption, since attractiveness is called not a report about the world.
explanation.question_type_note: An assumption question is answered by negation. Take each option, suppose the opposite, and see whether the argument still stands; only the necessary assumption brings it down.
explanation.reading_habit: Find the step in an argument where a new category appears, and ask what has to be true about that category for the step to work. That is where the unstated premise is sitting.

distractors.why_wrong: The second paragraph is about what believing is and mentions no tradition at all. Traditions arrive in the third paragraph, as the target of a conclusion the passage goes on to reject, and the fourth paragraph says most of what a religion asks is practice rather than assent.
distractors.seductive_element: The passage as a whole is about religious demands, so a premise about them looks like the ground the argument stands on.

distractors.why_wrong: The argument needs no historical claim of any kind, and one this absolute would be far more than it needs. It shows why the thing cannot be done from what believing is, which makes the record of attempts irrelevant to it.
distractors.seductive_element: It sounds like the strongest possible version of the conclusion, and a reader who is looking for what the argument requires may reach for what would settle it instead.

distractors.why_wrong: This is the passage's first qualification, argued for in the fourth paragraph, not a premise of the second. Negating it leaves the conceptual argument entirely intact: belief would still be unchosen, and would simply also be unmanageable.
distractors.seductive_element: It is the live rival, because it is a claim the author certainly holds, and readers looking for an assumption often pick the author's most important other commitment.

questions.target_mistake: characterising the passage by the use the third paragraph describes, which the passage exists to refuse
questions.prediction_target: The learner should be able to name the move in a verb and an object: establish what believing is, then limit what that establishes.
questions.stem: Which of the following best characterises the passage as a whole?

options.A: an argument that the demands religious traditions place on their members are incoherent
options.B: a defence of believers against the charge that they have chosen their beliefs carelessly
options.C: a claim about what believing is, followed by a careful account of how little it settles
options.D: a comparison of two routes to belief, with a verdict in favour of the slower of the two

explanation.expert_notice: The passage divides at the third paragraph, which says the premise is sound, the conclusion does not follow, and three things need saying. Everything before it establishes the claim; everything after it restricts what the claim can be used for, and the restriction takes more space than the claim.
explanation.correct_reasoning: The correct option keeps the two halves in that order and in that proportion. The claim is conceptual, that believing is taking something to be so; the restriction is that this covers only the moment of assent, leaves the believer open to appraisal, and stops short of licensing any demand for a result. An option that keeps the claim without the restriction describes the first two paragraphs alone.
explanation.question_type_note: A best-characterisation question wants a verb and an object, both of which must survive the last paragraph. Where a passage spends more space qualifying a claim than making it, the qualifying is part of what the passage is.
explanation.reading_habit: Count the paragraphs on each side of a passage's turn. The proportion tells you which half the author thought was the contribution, and characterisation questions follow the proportion.

distractors.why_wrong: This is the inference the third paragraph reports and refuses, saying the conclusion does not follow. The final paragraph then names a demand that is perfectly coherent, since go and study for a year is something a person can do and fail at.
distractors.seductive_element: It is the live rival, because the first two paragraphs build exactly this case, and readers who reach the third paragraph with the conclusion already formed take the refusal for a hedge.

distractors.why_wrong: No such charge is discussed and no defence is offered. The passage moves the other way in its second qualification, saying the position leaves a believer open to appraisal rather than beyond it.
distractors.seductive_element: A passage arguing that belief is not chosen sounds as though it must be excusing somebody, and the subject matter makes a defence the expected genre.

distractors.why_wrong: The two routes are not offered as alternatives to be ranked. The passage says the direct route does not exist at all, and the indirect one is described precisely to show that it is not a route to a chosen destination.
distractors.seductive_element: The passage does set a direct route against an indirect one, so a reader who has the contrast right will supply the verdict such contrasts usually end in.

questions.target_mistake: turning the demand for attention into a demand for the belief that attention was supposed to produce
questions.prediction_target: The learner should predict that the inference will concern what an instruction can and cannot require, since the passage ends by separating the looking from the landing.
questions.stem: Which of the following can most reasonably be inferred from the passage?

options.A: An instruction to go and examine the evidence can be obeyed in a way that an instruction to believe cannot
options.B: A person who has attended carefully and still does not believe has failed at something he was asked to do
options.C: Traditions that ask for practice rather than for assent have understood the point the passage makes
options.D: Any belief a person now holds can be traced back to a decision he once took about what to read

explanation.expert_notice: The last three sentences do the work. What can be asked is the looking; what cannot be asked is the landing; and a tradition that says go and study has asked for something a person can do, and fail at, and be judged on, while one that says believe this has asked for something nobody can hand over.
explanation.correct_reasoning: The correct option is that division stated as a claim about instructions. An instruction is obeyable when the thing demanded is within the agent's power, and the passage has spent two paragraphs establishing that the attending is and the assent is not. Nothing is added, and in particular nothing is said about whether obedience will produce the belief.
explanation.question_type_note: An inference question rewards the option that keeps a distinction the author has just drawn. Where a passage separates what may be required from what may not, the inference will be about the requiring.
explanation.reading_habit: When an author ends by dividing two things that had been treated as one, state the division in your own words before reading the options. Most wrong answers in such questions quietly reunite them.

distractors.why_wrong: The fifth paragraph rules this out in the sentence that sets up its division, saying a person who attends properly may end where he began and that nothing in his attending guarantees the outcome. The failure would have to lie in the landing, which cannot be asked for.
distractors.seductive_element: The passage does say a person can fail at what is asked, and a reader who takes the belief to be what was asked will attach the failure to the wrong thing.

distractors.why_wrong: No claim is made about what any tradition has understood. The passage says what a tradition asks for when it asks for practice, which is a statement about the demand rather than about the insight of whoever framed it.
distractors.seductive_element: The closing sentences do praise one kind of demand over another, and readers convert approval of a practice into a compliment to the people who adopted it.

distractors.why_wrong: The fourth paragraph says the voluntary acts alter belief slowly and unreliably, which is a long way from making every belief the product of a decision. The passage's whole third point is that the connection falls short of a guarantee in either direction.
distractors.seductive_element: It is the tidy general form of the passage's qualification, and a reader who has just learned that attention shapes belief will want to state the discovery as a rule.

vocabulary.passage_use: the claim covers the moment of assent and nothing else
vocabulary.meaning_here: the act of accepting something as true

vocabulary.passage_use: The testimony of somebody who was there
vocabulary.meaning_here: what a witness reports, offered as grounds for believing

vocabulary.passage_use: open to appraisal rather than beyond it
vocabulary.meaning_here: being judged, favourably or not, for what one has done

vocabulary.passage_use: Almost everything a religion actually asks of a person is voluntary
vocabulary.meaning_here: done by choice, and so capable of being required

mentor.challenge: The first half proves something and the second half spends longer saying what it does not prove. Work out where the turn is, because three of the four questions are decided after it.
mentor.one_sentence_summary: Nobody can believe something by deciding to, and the reason is conceptual rather than psychological, since believing is taking a thing to be so and only considerations bearing on whether it is so can move it, but this settles far less than it is usually made to settle, because attention and company are voluntary and do shape belief, because a believer can still be judged for what he arranged to avoid, and because the indirect route only places a person where a belief may arrive, so what can be demanded is the looking and never the landing.
mentor.main_idea: You cannot believe at will, and the reason is not weak willpower. To believe is to take something as true, so only evidence-like considerations can move belief, and an attractive conclusion is not one of those. This is usually used to say that religious demands are impossible to meet. It does not show that. What a person reads, where he goes and whose company he keeps are all voluntary and do shape belief over time, and he can be judged for how he arranged them. But arranging is not choosing: nothing guarantees the result. So the looking can be asked for and the belief cannot.
mentor.simple_explanation:
Try to believe, right now, that there is a second moon. Not pretend, not say it out loud, actually believe it. You cannot. And notice what kind of failure that is: it is not that you did not try hard enough. It is like trying to get taller by deciding to.

Why? Because of what believing is. To believe something is to take it that it is true. So the only things that can shift a belief are things that bear on whether it is true: evidence, an argument, somebody who was there telling you what he saw. What cannot shift it is how nice it would be if it were true. Offer somebody a fortune to believe in the second moon and you have given him a very strong motive and no reason at all, and the motive has nothing to grip. So the inability is not about willpower. It comes from what the thing is for.

Now, this argument usually gets used for something bigger. If you cannot choose what you believe, people say, then asking somebody to believe is asking the impossible, and any tradition that demands belief is demanding something nobody can supply. The first part is right. The conclusion does not follow, and there are three reasons.

First, the claim only covers the actual moment of accepting something as true. Nearly everything a religion actually asks you to do is a choice: where you go on Sunday morning, what you read and avoid reading, who you spend time with, what you give an hour a day to. All of those slowly and unreliably change what you end up believing. So belief is not chosen, but it is not unmanaged either.

Second, that leaves a believer open to judgement rather than safe from it. Someone who has carefully arranged never to hear a decent argument against his view has done something, and that something was a choice, even if what he now thinks is not.

Third, and this is the sharpest bit, the slow route is not a slower way of choosing. It is a way of putting yourself in a place where a belief might arrive. Somebody who reads and listens properly may end up exactly where he started, or somewhere he did not want to be, and nothing about doing the work guarantees a result.

So here is the line that follows. You can be asked to do the looking. You cannot be asked to do the landing. Go and study this, sit with these people, give it an hour a day for a year: that is something a person can do, and fail to do, and be judged on. Believe this: that is asking for something nobody can hand over, no matter how much they want to.
mentor.why_difficult: The first two paragraphs make a clean and satisfying argument, and the rest of the passage is about what that argument does not license, so a reader who fixes the position early will characterise the passage by a conclusion it explicitly refuses. The second difficulty is that the three qualifications do not all pull the same way: the first two enlarge what can be asked of a believer and the third pulls it back, and the crucial division between the looking and the landing arrives only in the final three sentences. The third is the word may, which carries the whole of the third point and is easy to read as though it denied any connection at all.
mentor.author_intention: To settle a question about what believing is, and then to stop the settlement being spent on a larger conclusion it does not cover, so that the reader ends holding both the impossibility of the demand to believe and the good sense of the demand to look.

paragraph_journey.note: Try to believe in a second moon and you cannot. The interesting thing is what kind of failure that is: not one more effort would fix.
Believing is taking something to be true, so only what bears on truth can move it. An attractive conclusion is a motive with nothing to grip.
The claim gets used to show that religious demands are impossible. The premise is sound; the conclusion does not follow, and three things need saying.
It covers only the moment of assent, and nearly everything a religion asks is voluntary. And a believer can still be judged for what he arranged to avoid.
The slow route only puts you where a belief may arrive; nothing guarantees it. So the looking can be asked for and the landing cannot.

mentor.tone_progression: It opens with the briskness of a demonstration, becomes analytical and flat while the explanation is given, turns careful at the point where the claim is taken away from the use it is usually put to, and ends measured and exact, dividing what may be demanded from what may not in short sentences.
key_transitions: 'The premise is sound. The conclusion does not follow from it, and three things need saying.' (close of paragraph 3) — the passage turns from proving a claim to limiting it.
'Belief is unchosen; it is not unmanaged.' (paragraph 4) — the first qualification in six words.
'What can be asked of somebody is the looking. What cannot be asked is the landing.' (paragraph 5) — the division the whole passage has been building towards.
mentor.misunderstanding: The commonest wrong model has the passage arguing that religious demands are impossible to meet, which is the inference the third paragraph reports and immediately refuses, and which the final paragraph contradicts by naming a demand that is perfectly meetable. The second wrong model comes from the phrase about a belief happening to a person: readers take it to mean that beliefs arrive at random, when the paragraph before has said what a person reads and whose company he keeps do alter what he believes. What the phrase removes is the guarantee, not the influence.
mentor.traps_summary: The set offers a refused conclusion as the passage's own, a later qualification as a premise of the earlier argument, the absence of any connection in place of the absence of a guarantee, and a failure attached to the belief rather than to the attending. Sorting each option into claim, reported use, qualification or division answers all four.
mentor.reading_lesson: When a passage proves something in two paragraphs and then spends three saying what the proof does not establish, the second half is the contribution and the first is the setup. Read the sentence that performs the turn, usually one that grants a premise and denies a conclusion, and treat everything after it as the author's real position. The same habit protects you from the other common error here: a word like may often removes a guarantee while leaving a connection standing, and the difference between those two is where the hardest option in such a set will live.
mentor.real_world: The same division runs through anything that can be required of a person only up to the point where the result stops being in their hands: a court can require disclosure and not a change of mind, an employer can require a training course and not enthusiasm, a teacher can require attention and not understanding. In each case the demand is intelligible exactly as far as the action reaches.
mentor.takeaway: You can be told where to look; you cannot be told what to find there.
mentor.reflection_question: Which of the things you have been asked to believe were really requests that you go and look at something?
